newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to trade restructured debt bonds of regions.
newsitem.headline: Russia to trade restructured debt bonds of regions.

text.p: Russian regions owing money to the federal government will be able to restructure their debt into securities which will be issued and traded on a new market, a senior Finance Ministry official said on Thursday.
The Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) will start trading the bonds issued by Russian debtor regions in June, said Bella Zlatkis, head of the Finance Ministry's securities department.
Trying to untangle a vast web of debt between companies, state and regions, and force payment of tax arrears, Russia has been forging ahead in recent weeks with initiatives to restructure debt.

A government order earlier this year allows companies to restructure tax debts either by issuing bonds or by issuing new equity comprising a controlling stake, to be held as collateral by the state, and several companies intend to use the option.
But Thursday's announcement was the first indication that similar options would be available to regional governments.
Zlatkis said 210 different securities, placed by over 70 issuers and with a total value of around nine trillion roubles, would trade on the exchange.
She said the bonds will be issued from June in equal tranches with maturities of one, two, and three years and an annual coupon rate of 10 percent.

The volume of the market is small in comparison with that for government securities, where the government typically issues 12 trillion roubles of paper a week, and daily trading volume can be around six trillion roubles.
Russia's third largest bank Uneximbank will act as depositary bank for the bonds, while Avtobank, Bank MFK, Natsionalny Reservny Bank, Bank Rossiisky Kredit and Unikombank will service the bonds.
Recent low yields on the government bond and treasury bill market were also forcing banks to look for new and promising, if as yet underdeveloped markets, Zlatkis said.
Under the government programme for enterprises, companies owing money to the state are allowed to securitise their debt by converting it into asset-backed securities.

These bonds are then transferred to the government as collateral. The company must pay off the tax debt and accumulated funds in regular installments, and if it falls behind the government can sell the bonds.
